tone_statements.citation: Hodieb, Liliane. 2024. On the syntax-prosody interface in Wushi (Babessi): Tone pattern, dissimilation and spreading. In James Essegbey, Brent Henderson, Fiona McLaughlin & Michael Diercks (eds.), Pushing the boundaries: Selected papers from the 51-52 Annual Conference on African Linguistics (Contemporary African Linguistics), 163-184. Berlin: Language Science Press. doi:10.5281/zenodo.14038745
tone_statements.quote: Underlyingly, Wushi has four tones: two level tones H (high) and L (low) inherited from the proto language – they were reconstructed for Proto-Grassfields (Watters 2003: 236) – and two contour tones that were phonologized in the language, LH (rising) and HL (falling). Surface tones are H, L, M (mid), HL (falling), LH (rising), and HM, plus downstepped ꜜH, ꜜM and ꜜHM. [...] The mora is the tone bearing unit in the language.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 164-165, sec. 2 'The lexical tone system' (TBU sentence on p. 165)
tone_statements.n_tones: 4 underlying (H, L, LH, HL); surface H, L, M, HL, LH, HM + downstepped H, M, HM

tone_statements.citation: Robinson, Rachel. 2022. Wushi (Babessi) Orthography Proposal. Yaoundé: SIL. 41 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 92907.
tone_statements.quote: All verb roots in Wushi have either underlying high tone or underlying low tone (Robinson 2021: 18-19). … Tone marking for verbs is illustrated in the table below, using minimal tone pairs to demonstrate the contrast between underlyingly high and underlyingly low verb roots: … /bvə/ bvə give birth bvə̀ fall … Tone on nouns in Wushi is very complex. A provisional study looking at surface tone on 250 nouns in isolation (Robinson 2018: 44-50) found that there are: five distinctive tone patterns for monosyllabic nouns … seven distinctive tone patterns for disyllabic nouns
tone_statements.locator: pp. 17-18 sec. 3.1 'Marking lexical tone on verbs' and p. 19 sec. 3.2 'Marking lexical tone on nouns'
tone_statements.summary: Verb roots contrast underlying high vs low tone (minimal pairs); verb suffixes toneless; nouns show 5-7 surface tone patterns, unanalysed; floating tonal morphemes mark perfective, irrealis, hortative.

tone_statements.citation: Robinson, Rachel. 2018. [Phonological sketch of Wushi]. SIL Cameroon, unpublished ms. (cited in Hodieb 2021: 45)
tone_statements.quote: Surface tone was marked on 70 monosyllabic nouns, i.e. monosyllabic noun roots with a non-segmental noun class affix. Five distinctive tone patterns were found. … The two distinctive surface patterns for tone on verbs have been called ‘high’ and ‘low rising’. All verbs can be divided into these two categories. The underlying tones of the two categories are, though, a matter for further research. … The five distinctive patterns in Wushi are high, low falling, low, high-mid and high-low.
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone: five distinctive surface tone patterns on monosyllabic noun roots (high, low falling, low, high-mid, high-low), two on verbs (high, low rising); underlying tone left for later research.

sources.citation: Akumbu, Pius W. 2024. Review of Liliane Hodieb, Description du wushi, langue grassfields du Cameroun. Linguistique et langues africaines 10(2). doi:10.4000/13lt3
sources.note: Summarises the book's phonology: segmental phonology ch. 1 (pp. 49-87), tonology ch. 2 (pp. 89-134); four underlying tones H, L, HL, LH; surface H, L, M, HL, LH, HM, downstepped M and H; mostly monosyllabic roots, CV(ʔ) syllables. The words stress/accent/prominence do not occur in the review. (Anubis blocks automated download; paragraphs 3-4 transcribed from direct download output into the.)

sources.citation: Hodieb, Liliane. 2021. On the aspectual system of Wushi (Babessi), a Ring Grassfields Bantu language of Cameroon. Language in Africa 2(2): 43-65. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2021-2-2-43-65
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Verb section treats tone as grammatical: 'a consistent LH tone on the verb is actually the perfective marker; thus, it is tonally marked rather than segmentally marked' (p. 47); 'There is a constraint in the language that prevents more than two L tones from occurring successively' (p. 53). Also reports (p. 45) an unpublished 2018 SIL Cameroon phonological sketch of Wushi by Robinson.
